description: We're two Green Hope High School students trying to build something great.
summary: Apollo 1 showed that cabin air decides how deadly a fire is, and Artemis plans Moon bases at 30% oxygen or more, yet NASA certifies materials with a 1-g fire test. We ask whether that test can be trusted there. We report three new results from NASA data. First, we restored the missing outcomes of 124 BASS-II fire tests on the ISS from NASA's report. Second, we mapped every PSI test condition and found zero solid-material tests at Moon-base air: PSI's ISS solid tests stop at 22.2% O₂. Third, we built a checker that flags which Earth-rated materials need re-testing. In NASA drop-tower tests, thin films burned in microgravity at up to 3.9 points less oxygen than the 1-g test allows, so any thin material rated 30–33.9% on Earth is suspect for a 30% Moon base. Each number traces to a NASA table cell or a verbatim quote. An SI-powered dashboard turns the results into briefs for five habitats and suggests the next experiments to fly.
details:
What it does

Flame in Freefall is a free website that helps engineers decide which cabin materials need more fire testing before they go to the Moon or Mars.

NASA approves materials with a fire test done on Earth, but some thin materials that pass that test keep burning in weightlessness, and Moon bases are planned with more oxygen than the air we breathe.

On the website, you enter a material's Earth test result and pick a habitat: a Moon base, a Mars base, a rover, the space station or a spacecraft cabin. The site tells you whether the material is safe there, fails, or should be re-tested in weightlessness.

It also ranks NASA's 24 space fire experiments by how useful they are for that habitat, answers plain-English questions with quotes from NASA reports, and suggests which experiment to fly next.

How it works

We gathered every combustion experiment in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics database and pulled measurements from 84 NASA reports (We kept a measurement only if the sentence it came from appears word for word in the report) and linked every number on the site back to its source.

We then used NASA's own formula for the oxygen safety margin to compare Earth and space results.
Note: NASA's database also lists 129 space station burn tests without saying what happened, thus we filled in 124 of those results from NASA's written report.

Benefits and impact

In NASA's drop-tower tests, thin films and fabrics burned in weightlessness at up to 3.9 points less oxygen than the Earth test predicts.

For a Moon base at 30% oxygen, that means any thin material that passes the Earth test only between 30% and 33.9% should be tested again.

We also (non-exhaustively) found that NASA's public data has no fire tests of solid materials at Moon-base oxygen levels. We hope the site helps NASA and its partners choose what to test before Artemis crews live in that air, and gives students and researchers one place to explore NASA's fire data.

Tools we used

We used Python and python libraries (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and matplotlib) for the data pipeline and models. For our website, we used TypeScript with React, Vite and Tailwind as the frontend, and it is hosted for free on GitHub Pages.

We utilized a small search model (MiniLM) that runs inside the browser for our 'Search' page in the website.

We used LaTex in our report and execute brief.

We used HyperFrames for the video, and Kokoro-82M, an open-weight text-to-speech model to generate the synthetic voice for the video (we were unfortunately not allowed to be in the video, as we were minors).

We used no special hardware, just our laptops.

What makes it creative

We think that we made it creative by turning NASA's safety-margin formula into a check anyone can run on one material.

We did it by recovering test results missing from NASA's database by reading NASA's own reports. And the question tool we implemented answers only with quotes and numbers from NASA sources rather than writing its own text, straying from hallucination-prone LLMs.

What we considered

We considered stopping once we reached the '3.9' figure for the disparity between Earth testing and Lunar conditions. However, we saw we had extra time and implemented a lot more than we thought we could in such a short time.

We considered voicing our video, but after emailing Space Apps, we were told that because we're both minors, the video should use a synthetic voice (SI). We (of-course) specified it in the video and description.
